1:
Gill places the speech not on the mount during the forty days but after Moses came down and the tabernacle was set up, while Israel still lay encamped about the mountain; the words may be rendered by or near Mount Sinai, and Josephus reports these laws delivered while Israel lay encamped under it. Wesley agrees that the particle bears the sense of near, so that there is no need to disturb the history here, and Ellicott takes the mountain for the mountainous tract rather than the peak. Ellicott thinks the chapter itself out of place: it should have followed the chapter on the festivals, since the sabbatical year and the jubilee are closely connected with those regulations, and the isolation of these ordinances can be explained on no other principle than the one laid down by the second Temple authorities, that many of the sections are transposed and there is no strict sequence in the Law. Keil sets the institution beside the weekly one: as the nation at large, with its labourers and beasts of burden, kept a Sabbath every seventh day, so the land was to keep a Sabbath to the Lord — six years they were to cultivate corn-fields, vineyards and olive-yards, and in the seventh the land was to keep a rest consecrated to him, neither tilled nor reaped.

Henry finds several reasons in the law at once. God would hereby show them that he was their landlord and they tenants at will under him, since landlords stipulate with their tenants when they shall break up their ground and when they shall let it rest; it was besides a kindness to the land to let it rest, and would keep it in heart, as our husbandmen say, for a posterity whose satisfaction God would have them consult. They were brought besides to live in dependence upon divine providence, finding that as man lives not by bread alone, so he has bread not by his own industry alone. Clarke turns the practical objection into an argument. If it required all the annual produce of the field to support the inhabitants, how could the people be nourished in the seventh year, when no produce was received? God sent his blessing in an especial manner on the sixth year, which brought forth fruit for three; and the miracle speaks for itself, proving the divine authenticity of the law — for no man in his senses, without God's authority, could have made such an ordinance, since the sixth year would have amply refuted his pretensions to a divine mission.

What counted as cultivation Ellicott answers from the same canons. No one was allowed in the sabbatical year to plant trees, to cut off dried-up branches, to break off withered leaves, to smoke under the plants in order to kill the insects, or to besmear unripe fruit with soil to protect it, and anyone who did received the prescribed number of stripes; as much land, however, might be cultivated as was needed for the payment of taxes, and for the barley of the wave sheaf and the wheat for the two wave-loaves. Keil explains whose the produce was: what grew of itself was not to be reaped by the owner, but masters and servants, labourers and visitors, cattle and game alike were to eat of it away from the field, so that it became common to all. Exodus assigns it to the poor and needy, but the owner is nowhere forbidden to partake as well, so that no discrepancy can be discovered. Henry closes on what the year figured, the spiritual rest believers enter through Christ, our true Noah, who gives us comfort concerning our work and the toil of our hands because of the ground the Lord hath cursed — and as the fruits of this sabbath were enjoyed in common, so the salvation wrought by Christ is a common salvation.
8:
Whether the jubilee fell on the forty-ninth year or the fiftieth is their chief dispute. Henry holds for the forty-ninth, which by a very common form of speech is called the fiftieth, and refers the argument to the chronologer Calvisius; he notes that seven sabbaths of weeks were reckoned from passover to pentecost, itself called the fiftieth day. Clarke allows either reading, supposing Moses may include the preceding jubilee and so make up fifty with the forty-ninth, or that he speaks of proclaiming it on the forty-ninth and celebrating it on the fiftieth; some place it on the forty-ninth to keep it from being confounded with the sabbatical year, but he thinks the fiftieth the real jubilee. Ellicott reads the phrase as count seven weeks of years, the seven days of each week standing for so many years; and he reports the second Temple reckoning, that since the first sabbatical year fell in the twenty-first year after the entrance into Canaan, the first jubilee fell in the sixty-fourth. Wesley argues from usage: the weekly sabbath is called the seventh day because it truly was so, being next after the six and distinct from them all; in like manner the jubilee is called the fiftieth because it comes next after seven times seven and is distinct from them all.

What the name means they are no more agreed upon. Gill weighs three derivations — from the peculiar sound of the trumpet; from the instrument itself, which the Jews suppose a ram's horn, jobel in Arabic signifying a ram; or, as he thinks best, from the verb to bring back, because at this time men were returned to their liberty, estates and families. Keil looks past the etymology to what the blast recalled. The far-reaching horn had been the signal of the Lord's descent upon Sinai, to raise Israel to be his people; and as they came up to the mountain at that sound, so at the expiration of the forty-nine years the same blast went through the land to proclaim the year's entrance.

Henry marks the day chosen for it. The trumpet was sounded at the close of the day of atonement, and very fitly: when they had been humbling and afflicting their souls for sin, then they were made to hear this voice of joy and gladness, and when their peace was made with God, then liberty was proclaimed — for the removal of guilt is necessary to make way for the entrance of all true comfort. In allusion to that proclamation, he says, it was foretold of our Lord Jesus that he should preach the acceptable year of the Lord. Ellicott presses the same connection to its moral: at the close of the great Day of Atonement, when the Hebrew realised that his heavenly Father had annulled his sins, he was called to proclaim by nine blasts of the cornet that he too had freed every encumbered family estate — inasmuch as God has forgiven his debts, he also is to forgive his debtors. Calvin calls this the most illustrious of the three sabbaths, since by it the state of the people, as to persons and houses and property alike, was renewed; it was an imposing memorial of the sacred rest to see slaves suddenly emancipated, houses and lands returning to the possessors who had sold them, and all things assuming a new face — though its main feature, he insists, was the solemnity showing them a people separated from other nations, that being redeemed anew they might devote themselves entirely to God their Deliverer. Wesley finds a further use in it, that inheritances, families and tribes might be kept entire until the Messiah came, who was to be known by the tribe and family out of which he came; since when, he says, those characters are miserably confounded — no small argument that the Messiah is come.
11:
Gill takes this verse to settle the question. That a jubilee shall that fiftieth year be shows it was not the forty-ninth, as many learned men have asserted, induced chiefly by the reason that two years would then come together in which there was neither sowing nor reaping; but God, who could cause the earth to bring forth fruit for three years, could make it bring forth enough for four. To make their opinion agree with this passage, he says, they must reckon the foregoing jubilee as one of the fifty and begin their account thence — which could not be done in the first account of the jubilee at all. Ellicott reports the same as the unanimous testimony of the second-Temple authorities, Philo and Josephus among them, and draws the consequence: as the forty-ninth year is the sabbatical year and the fiftieth the jubilee, there were two successive fallow years. Clarke turns to the name and finds it unsettled. Josephus says it signifies liberty, but that is rather the intention of the institution than the meaning of the term; the rabbins say a ram's horn, because the trumpets were made of them, but no ancient version acknowledges that sense except the Chaldee. The most natural derivation, he judges, is from a verb meaning to bring back or recall, since estates that had been alienated were then brought back to their primitive owners. He adds that this wise and excellent institution appears to have been little regarded after the Babylonish captivity, and must have ceased altogether when the Jews were brought under a foreign yoke.

Clarke reads the whole as typical of two things. First of the great time of release, the Gospel dispensation, when all who believe in Christ Jesus are redeemed from the bondage of sin and repossess the favour and image of God, having all debts cancelled and the right of inheritance restored — to which he thinks Isaiah alludes. Second of the general resurrection, which Parkhurst calls a lively prefiguration of the grand consummation, introduced in like manner by the trump of God. It is worthy of remark, Clarke adds, that the jubilee was not proclaimed until the very day when the great annual atonement was made for the sins of the people — and does not this prove that the liberty published under the Gospel could not take place till the sacrifice of the Lord Jesus had been offered up?

On the sale of land the law forbids overreaching, and Clarke states the ground sharply: they were to take no advantage of each other's ignorance in buying or selling, for he that buys an article at less than it is worth, or sells one for more, is no better than a thief, since he actually robs his neighbour of as much property as he has bought below or sold above its current value. Wesley puts both sides: neither is the seller to require more, nor the buyer to take advantage of his brother's necessities to give him less than the worth of it. Ellicott reports how the rule was enforced: if anyone bought or sold a thing for a sixth part more than its value, the aggrieved party might have the excess returned, and if the difference exceeded a sixth the contract could be rescinded altogether. On the pricing itself the three agree. Clarke likens it to buying the unexpired term of a lease among us, the purchase being regulated by the years of the current jubilee still unelapsed; Keil says the same, that they were to sell only the produce of the yearly revenues up to the next jubilee, making the price higher or lower according to the number of years; and Ellicott presses the vendor's side, that he sells not the land but a certain number of crops, so that the fallow sabbatical years falling within the term are not counted among them.
20:
Gill takes the objection for what it betrays: it is the speech of such as are of little faith, who disbelieve the promise and indulge an anxiety how they shall be fed in a year when there is neither tillage of land nor pruning of trees. Clarke calls it a very natural question, which only the sovereign promise of the next verse could lay to rest. Calvin makes more of the difficulty. Men will never be obedient to God's precepts unless their distrust of him is corrected, he says, and will always be ingenious in laying hold of pretexts for disobedience; yet here the difficulty was a specious excuse, for famine might have destroyed them in those two years — and whence were they to get seed to sow after the land had rested a whole year? Not without reason, then, does God deliver them from this doubt by promising such abundance in the sixth year as should suffice for the two following; and the phrase is to be observed, that he would command his blessing beyond the usual course, so that the land should be twice or thrice more fertile.

How the three years are counted Ellicott and Wesley reckon alike. Wesley makes it not three complete years but in great part — the portion of the sixth year between harvest and the beginning of the seventh, the whole of the seventh, and the portion of the eighth before harvest; and this is added, he says, to show the equity of the command, for as God would hereby try their faith, so he gave an eminent proof of his own exact providence. Ellicott counts the same three portions and draws the parallel with the manna: as at the institution of the weekly Sabbath God sent down a double portion every sixth day to make up for the day of rest, so he exercises a special providence every sixth year by blessing the soil with a treble crop. He notices that the question properly applies to the eighth year rather than the seventh, since the seventh is supplied by the harvest of the sixth.

On the ground of the prohibition they are of one mind. Keil states the rule in its own words: the land shall not be sold litsmithuth, literally to annihilation, that is, so as to vanish away from or be for ever lost to the seller; and the same verse lays down how a man compelled by poverty to sell his patrimony was to recover it by redemption. Henry says that God, having a particular propriety in this land, would by the restraint keep them sensible of it; and that since they were strangers and sojourners with him there, having his tabernacle among them, to alienate their part would be in effect to cut themselves off from communion with God, of which it was the token. Clarke says they were to consider themselves merely tenants to the great landholder, and thinks the arrangement favourable to religion, since men who feel they have nothing they can call their own on earth must often be put in mind of a permanent dwelling in the heavenly inheritance. Calvin warns that the reason for this law was peculiar to the children of Abraham and can hardly be applied to other nations, since the land was divided by lot as though God had by his own hand located them in their stations. Henry finds the gospel in the office of the kinsman: he is called Goel, the redeemer, to whom belonged the right of redeeming the land, and this typified Christ, who assumed our nature that he might be our kinsman, bone of our bone, and who, being the only kinsman we have that is able to do it, has the right of redemption — for as to all our other kinsmen, their shoe must be plucked off, since they cannot redeem.
24:
Ellicott draws the consequence of the tenancy: being simply tenants at will, the land is not even to remain with the purchaser until the jubilee, but the buyer is to grant the seller every opportunity of redeeming it before that time. Calvin marks how far the permission goes beyond what other nations allowed. Before the jubilee came, God permits not only the relations to redeem land sold by a poor man, but the seller himself, if no other redeemer interposed; the like power was given to relations among other peoples, though with a different object, the preservation of the family name, and there the seller was never allowed to redeem unless a special clause stood in the contract. God desired that the lands should be retained by their legal possessor, so that the people might deviate as little as possible from the division made under Joshua; and in the perpetual succession, Calvin says, he considered himself rather than men, that the recollection of his kindness should never be lost. Keil states the last of the three cases: if a man had not earned as much as was required to make compensation for the recovery of his land, what he had sold was to remain with the buyer until the jubilee, and then to go out.

That poverty alone can justify the sale they both infer from the wording. Ellicott observes that poverty is the only reason the Law here supposes might lead a man to part with his field, from which the second-Temple authorities concluded that no one may sell his patrimony on speculation — which accounts, he says, for the horror Naboth expressed to Ahab at giving away the inheritance of his fathers. Gill draws the same rule and cites Maimonides: no man may sell his field unless his distress presses him and forces him to it, nor sell his estate to put money into his purse, or to trade with, or to purchase goods or cattle, but only for food. On the reckoning of the redemption money Gill sets out the arithmetic — count how many years have passed since the sale and how many remain to the jubilee, so that if just half the time is gone, half the price is repaid to the purchaser, and if the halves are unequal, then in proportion.

On the kinsman-redeemer Clarke, Wesley and Ellicott converge. Clarke notes that the kinsman is called in the text goel, the redeemer, and asks whether this was not a lively emblem of the redemption of man by Christ Jesus: that he might have a right to redeem man he took upon him human nature, and became a kinsman of the great family of the human race, thereby possessing the right of redeeming that fallen nature of which he took part. Wesley says the same in a clause, that the redeemer here was an eminent type of Christ, made near akin to us by taking our flesh that he might perform the work of redemption for us. Ellicott fills out the office from elsewhere in the Law: the word is applied to one who, by virtue of being nearest of kin, had not only to redeem the patrimony but to marry the childless widow of his brother and to avenge his blood. Ellicott closes on what the whole provision was for. Its design was to secure to each family a permanent interest in the soil and to prevent the accumulation of land in the hands of the greedy few who are ever anxious to join field unto field, precluding both landless beggars and too extensive landed proprietors; and similar laws obtained among other nations of antiquity, Solon making it a law that no one should acquire as much land as he wished, while Plato held that no individual should possess more than four times the quantity held by the lowest owner.
29:
Clarke explains the difference put between a city house and a country one. The city house might be built for trade merely, whereas the country house was attached to the inheritance which God had divided among the families, so that the same law had to apply to the house as to the inheritance. Presuming the city house to be for trade, he reasons on both sides: when a man had bought such a house and established his business there it would have been inconvenient to remove, yet the former owner might have sold rashly or under some urgent necessity, and so a year was allowed him to reconsider or to get through the necessity that forced it. The purchaser, on the other hand, must have been at great expense to fit the place for his work; and without some certainty of permanent possession, no such purchases would ever have been made. Ellicott grounds the distinction higher up: houses in walled cities are not the creation of God allotted by his command to the tribes, but the work of man, who builds them up and razes them at his own will, so that the law of jubilee does not apply to these temporary buildings.

Calvin argues the exception from the nature of the two properties. A house does not supply daily food as a field does, so it is more tolerable to be without a house than without a field. But the country houses had to be excepted, being appendages to the land: what use in harvesting the fruits, he asks, if you had no place to store them, and how could oxen plough without stalls in the neighbourhood? Lands without farm-buildings being almost useless, God justly appointed that every rural possession should revert in the jubilee to its former owner. Wesley gives the reasons why city houses were not to revert: the grounds alleged for lands do not hold here, since no confusion of tribes could follow the alienation of houses; the seller had besides a greater propriety in a house than in land, it being commonly built by his own cost and diligence; and God would hereby encourage men to possess houses in such places, since fulness of inhabitants in cities was a great strength to the whole land.

On the Levites Clarke anticipates the objection and turns it round. A Levite could not ultimately sell his house, and why — because Moses framed his laws so much in favour of the priesthood? Just the reverse: they were so far from being peculiarly favoured that they had no inheritance in Israel at all, only their cities to dwell in; and because their houses in those cities were the whole they could call their own, these could not be ultimately alienated. All they had to live on besides was that most precarious support, the freewill-offerings of the people, which depended on the prevalence of pure religion in the land. Calvin adds a public reason: the provision was made not only out of favour to the Levites but because it concerned the whole people that they should be posted like sentries in the place God had assigned them; the pasture lands were made inalienable for the same cause. Keil and Gill explain the pasture rule from the holding itself. Keil says the meadows were not saleable, nor even to be let until the jubilee, because if sold the Levites would have nothing left to feed their cattle upon; and Gill notes that no Levite had a field of his own, the suburbs belonging to them in common, which is why they might not agree together to sell it. Ellicott suspects the text itself, thinking it more than probable that a negative particle has dropped out and that the clause originally stood, and if one of the Levites doth not redeem it — the Vulgate still has the negative.
35:
Keil and Ellicott both press the literal force of the phrase. The Hebrew is that his hand wavers or trembles beside thee, meaning that he is no longer able to sustain himself alone; and the command that follows, Keil says, is literally to lay hold of him — thou shalt take him by the arm to help him out of his misfortune. Ellicott draws the duty from the same figure: when his hand is thus trembling it is the business of every Israelite to support that weak hand and enable it to gain a livelihood, since the jubilee laws guard the future interest of the man driven by poverty to sell his patrimony, but he must live in the meantime until the year of restoration comes. Ellicott corrects the rendering of the next clause as well. It is not though he be a stranger or a sojourner, but as a stranger and a sojourner: the impoverished Israelite is not to be treated as an outcast because want has compelled him to part with his land, but is to receive the same consideration that strangers and sojourners receive, who like him hold no landed property of their own.

Henry sets the duty in the plainest terms. Poverty and decay are great grievances, and very common, for the poor we have always with us; and the relief commanded is of three kinds — by sympathy, in pitying the poor; by service, in doing for them; and by supply, in giving to them according to their necessity and our ability. He notes the argument the law itself uses against extortion, fear thy God, and the reason annexed, that they may live with thee, for they may yet be serviceable to thee: the rich can as ill spare the poor as the poor can spare the rich, and it becomes those that have received mercy to show mercy. Gill adds that the relief was not to stop at present necessity, but that money was to be lent to put the man in a way of business and get his living for the future, without requiring any interest for it.

On the two words for what may not be taken they are careful. Clarke observes that usury at present signifies unlawful interest for money, though properly it means the reward or compensation given for the use of a thing, and is principally spoken of money. Ellicott reports the definitions that obtained during the second Temple, which distinguished the two terms: if a man lends a shekel worth four denarii and receives five in return, or lends two sacks of wheat and receives three, that is usury, a charge upon money; whereas increase falls upon products, as when a dealer who has contracted to deliver wheat at twenty-five denarii takes it back at thirty and undertakes to give wine for it, though he has no wine at the time and may yet lose by the rise in wine. Wesley states the prohibition broadly, that all kinds of usury are in this case forbidden, whether of money or of victuals or of anything commonly lent upon condition of receiving it back with advantage and overplus; and he adds the limit of the case: if a man borrow in his necessity there can be no doubt this law is binding still, but it cannot be thought to bind where money is borrowed for the purchase of lands, for trade, or for other improvements, since there it is reasonable that the lender should share with the borrower in the profit. Gill says the same in fewer words, that the text speaks only of persons in poor and necessitous circumstances. Wesley narrows the other term too, taking the sojourner here to mean proselytes only, since of other strangers they were permitted to take usury.
39:
Henry states the principle the law rests on: a native Israelite was never to be made a bondman for perpetuity. If he sold himself through extreme poverty, and to one of his own nation, it was not to be looked upon that the master had as absolute a property in him as in a captive taken in war, who might be used, sold and bequeathed at pleasure like a man's cattle; he shall serve as a hired servant, of whom the master has the use only and not a despotic power. The reason given is that they are my servants — God does not make his servants slaves, and therefore their brethren must not; and the apostle applies the words spiritually, ye are bought with a price, be not the servants of men. Ellicott adds what the second-Temple authorities counted degrading work for an Israelite bondman: he must not attend his master at the bath, nor undo the latchets of his sandals. Keil marks the line the law draws: servants bought of foreign nations might be left as an inheritance to a man's children and slave-labour performed through them, but never through his brethren the children of Israel.

On the rigour forbidden the three are agreed and go beyond the letter. Gill observes that the word is the very one used of the Egyptians when they made Israel to serve, and seems designed to put them in mind of it, that they might abstain from usage towards their brethren which they had met with from their cruellest enemies. Clarke asks what rigorous service is and answers first from the Jews, service which is not determined, and service whereof there is no need; but much more is implied — labour beyond a man's strength, or too long continued, or in unhealthy places, or without sufficient food, is labour exacted with rigour and consequently inhuman, and this law is made not for the Mosaic dispensation only but for every people under heaven. Henry turns it upon the masters: both the servant's work and his usage must be such as befit a son of Abraham, and masters who are always hectoring and domineering over their servants, unreasonable in exacting work and in giving rebukes, forget that their own Master is in heaven — and what will they do when he rises up? Wesley presses the same clause: though thou fear not those who are in thy power and unable to right themselves, yet fear that God who has commanded thee to use them kindly, and who will avenge their cause if thou oppress them.

Calvin raises the difficulty of the two terms. Since liberty had already been granted the Hebrew servant in the seventh year, why is it here postponed to the fiftieth? Some answer that if the jubilee fell within the six years he must then be set free, though the term were not complete; but Calvin thinks that too forced, and the view which most approves itself to him is that moderation is here specially prescribed towards those slaves who stood most exposed to violence. Men would not have dared to oppress at pleasure servants soon to be free; but those who by having their ears bored had subjected themselves to the longer period would have been the more outrageously harassed had God not interposed — and this is confirmed, he says, by the command that the children should be set free along with their fathers, which did not take place in the seventh year. Henry closes on the release itself, which typified our redemption from the service of sin by the grace of God in Christ, whose truth makes us free — and he reports from the Jewish writers that the servants to be discharged expressed their joy for ten days before the trumpet sounded by feasting and wearing garlands on their heads, whence it is called the joyful sound.
44:
Gill and Ellicott read this as an answer to an objection. Since the Law forbids holding a brother as a bondman or putting him to the menial work of slaves, the Hebrews might fairly ask, as Jarchi puts it, who then shall I have to minister to me? — and the verse is the reply. Ellicott adds the limits on the permission: the Israelites were restricted to the Ammonites, Moabites, Edomites and Syrians who were their neighbours, and forbidden to buy any slaves at all from the seven nations in their midst, whom they were ordered to destroy. Calvin observes that what God here permits as regards strangers was everywhere customary among the Gentiles, that a master's power over his slaves should last not merely until his death but pass in perpetual succession to his children. The point to notice is the antithesis: ye shall make use of their service, but over his brother no man shall rule with rigour. From this a restraint was laid upon the Israelites, lest they should imperiously rule the children of Abraham and leave them not half their liberty in comparison with the Gentiles — not that a cruel exercise of power over strangers was allowed, but that God would have the race of Abraham, whose liberator he was, exempted by certain privileges from the common lot.

Ellicott reports how far even that permission was narrowed in practice. The second-Temple authorities enacted that the master's right over this kind of bondman is restricted to their labour, and that he may not barter with them, misuse them or put them to shame; if he maimed one he must set him free. In contrast the Hebrew bondmen are called brethren, co-religionists in temporary servitude who are nevertheless fellow-heirs with their masters in the land — whence the same authorities enacted that there must be no difference between the daily food, raiment and dwelling of the master and of his Hebrew slave. Of the stranger who might hold such a servant Ellicott notes that he had submitted only to the seven commandments given to Noah and had not joined the Jewish religion — which is why the Chaldee renders it, if the hand of an uncircumcised sojourner wax strong.

Keil marks the difference the case turns on: the servitude of an Israelite to a settler who had come to the possession of property, or to a non-Israelite dwelling in the land, was redeemable at any time; and the phrase ger toshab distinguishes the foreign sojourner here from the Israelitish one of verse thirty-five. Calvin sets out the redemption and its arithmetic. A power of redeeming is granted to the man's relatives, or, if he had earned his price, to himself, a calculation being made of the time remaining before the jubilee. If none of his family aided him, he was set free at the jubilee with the rest. Calvin observes that God so mitigates his law as to lay no unjust burden on sojourners, conceding more to them than to the natives, since a man who sold himself to his brethren went out free in the seventh year while his slavery under a sojourner extended to the fiftieth; and the object of the whole was that none whom God had adopted should be alienated from their race and so depart from his worship. Clarke calls the rule equitable to sojourner and Israelite alike: they were to reckon the years he must otherwise have served until the jubilee, take the current yearly wages of a servant, and multiply the remaining years by that sum, the aggregate being the price of his redemption. Wesley gives the ground of it in a clause: the allowance is proportioned to what is given a hired servant for the like term, because it is not properly the man's person but his work and labour that was sold.
51:
Gill finishes the arithmetic: if fewer years remain to the jubilee than the man has already served, the less is given for his redemption, so that where he has served fifteen and five remain, the price falls accordingly. Keil describes the condition he was kept in meanwhile — the buyer was to hold him as a labourer engaged by the year, not ruling over him with severe oppression; and the clause in thine eyes he takes to mean, so that thou, the nation addressed, seest it. Ellicott presses that clause further. As long as the man is in service his master must not treat him as a slave, but behave to him as to one who hires out his labour from year to year and will after a short time be his own master again. By in thy sight the Israelite is admonished not to be a tacit spectator of a Gentile owner's cruel treatment of his brother: though he is not to resent it in the way the Lawgiver himself once resented such a thing in Egypt, he is still to remonstrate with the cruel master and to invoke the protection of the powers that be. Wesley says the same: thou shalt not suffer it to be done, but whether magistrate or private person shalt take care according to thy capacity to get it remedied.

Over the next clause they divide on a point of translation. Gill notes that the Targum of Jonathan supplies the sense our version follows, in any of the years between the sale and the jubilee, and that Aben Ezra reads so; but others take the words to mean by these — that is, by the persons already named, his nearest of kin or himself — since the word years is not in the text at all, and the Vulgate, the Septuagint and the Oriental versions render it by these means or persons. Ellicott decides for that second reading without hesitation: better, if he be not redeemed by these, namely by the relations or the means indicated just above; and he adds the point of the whole provision, that the heathen master is to submit to the laws of jubilee as much as the Hebrew. Keil sums up what the year accomplished. It helped every Israelite who had fallen into poverty and slavery to the recovery both of his property and of his personal freedom, so that the whole community was restored to the original condition appointed for it by God; and yet, he insists, that restoration of the theocratic state was not the highest object of the year, since the observance of sabbatical rest throughout the whole land formed part of the liberty it proclaimed.

Clarke closes on the ends the institution served, reporting Calmet's summary. The motive of the law was to prevent the rich from oppressing the poor and reducing them to perpetual slavery; that they should not get possession of all the lands by purchase, mortgage, or at last usurpation; that debts should not be multiplied too much, lest the poor be entirely ruined; and that slaves should not continue always, they and their wives and children, in servitude. On the closing words Clarke marks how far the gospel goes beyond them: the Israelites were a typical people, representing those who are children of God by faith in Christ Jesus, but these last have a peculiarity of blessing, for they are not merely servants but sons — to which, he says, the apostle alludes in writing that thou art no more a servant but a son, and if a son then an heir of God through Christ. Gill reads the verse the same way, that those redeemed by the blood of Christ should not be perpetual servants to men; observing from the Targum of Jonathan's servants to my law that those redeemed by Christ are servants to his gospel.
